title: The week's rhythm
hook: weekday prayers, a weekend gurdwara, a weekly seva
tomorrow: what do you pray for a child who isn't born yet?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sohila and sleep: the sky as the plate, the lamps already lit. Sleep in praise. One whole day, dawn to dark. Now, a week.
screen: `SLEEP IN PRAISE.` → `ONE DAY DONE. NOW, A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Sunday night, a calendar app: color blocks for school, work, practice, a birthday, the dentist. Every block is a promise to someone. Sikhs who keep the full rhythm add a few blocks that don't move: the daily banis, a weekend visit to the gurdwara, a regular stretch of seva. Not more to carry. A shape to carry it in.
screen: `SUNDAY NIGHT, COLOR BLOCKS.` → `BLOCKS THAT DON'T MOVE.` → `A SHAPE TO CARRY IT IN.`

segments.voice: Start with the daily part: the banis at dawn and dusk and bedtime, the same words at the same doors. Then the weekly part, with other people. The sangat, the congregation. Guru Nanak asks, on ang 72, in paraphrase: how is the true congregation known? Where the One Name is spoken. Not by its size, or its building. Then seva, service done without pay: the langar kitchen, the shoe room, sweeping, washing dishes. On ang 26 Guru Nanak puts it plainly, in paraphrase: do seva in the middle of the world, and you'll find a place in the Lord's court. In the middle of the world, not after it. So what does the tradition give you for a crowded week? A rhythm, not a pile. A pile grows every time you add to it, and one missed day makes it feel ruined. A rhythm is a pattern you come back to. It bends in a hard week, a sick week, a week with a baby coming, and it still beats. Daily words, a weekly gathering, a regular piece of service.
screen: `DAILY: THE SAME WORDS.` · `WEEKLY: THE SANGAT.` · `SEVA, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORLD.` · `A RHYTHM, NOT A PILE.` · then, large: `A RHYTHM FOR THE WEEK.`

segments.voice: Open the coming week in your head. Choose one fixed time for prayer, one for gathering with others, and one for service. For each, name the thing most likely to crowd it out, and what you'll do when it does.
The week's rhythm. Daily banis, a weekly sangat, and regular seva, kept as a pattern you come back to.
Your line: a rhythm for the week. It bends, and it still beats. Have a good one.

screen: `DAY 1636 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 10 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DO YOU PRAY FOR A CHILD NOT YET BORN?`

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the full rhythm say the daily banis morning and evening, join the sangat at the gurdwara, often at a weekend diwan, and take a regular share of seva, in the langar, the shoe room or cleaning.

fork.setup: your friend builds a perfect week of prayer and service, misses Tuesday, and wants to quit. what does a rhythm offer her?
options: pick it up on Wednesday; a rhythm is the coming back, not a perfect streak.
start the whole plan over next Monday so the week counts from the beginning.
double Wednesday's prayers so the week's total still comes out the same.
fork.reveal: a pile feels ruined by one missed day; a rhythm bends and still beats.

chat.says: bhua's baby could come any day AND finals are next week. should i drop seva at the gurdwara this month?
options: shrink it, don't drop it: a rhythm bends in a hard week and still keeps its beat.
drop it: seva only counts when there's free time left over to give it.
change nothing: one skipped week breaks the rhythm for the whole year.
